items.title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef
items.description:
Two Rust types are both called PostingList, but changing them breaks different code. A text search finds both; a context graph preserves their identities and exposes their separate dependencies. Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender use that distinction to connect data engineering and coding agents. For a data system, valid SQL can still produce the wrong answer when a join multiplies rows or a refactor changes a metric's meaning. Michael describes a context layer that computes grain, lineage and relationships from transformation code, checks join assumptions against real data, and makes the resulting evidence queryable before an agent acts.

Callender builds a smaller version over selected crates in Qdrant. Tree sitter extracts syntax, Rustdoc resolves symbols, and Neo4j stores the relationships. An agent can then ask which symbols depend on a particular type instead of repeatedly searching files and inferring connections. The workshop's central complication comes next: given better graph tools, the agent may still choose grep. Tool naming, familiar output formats and prompting become part of the interface, and evaluations must measure whether the tools are actually used. Cached comparisons separate getting an answer right once from getting it right across repeated runs, while trace inspection catches flaws hidden by a favorable score. The closing discussion explores incremental indexing, Python's harder resolution problem, small auditable semantic operations with Fenic, and the work required to extend a classroom example into a maintained context layer.

items.title: Turning My Obsidian Vault Into a Local AI Engineer — Filip Makraduli, Superlinked
items.description:
A scanned NDA becomes a redacted Markdown document before a coding agent uses its contents. Filip Makraduli builds that workflow around an Obsidian vault, an MCP integration and Superlinked's inference engine, with small open models doing document processing on infrastructure the team controls. The starting problem combines sensitive files, expensive context and the need to adapt models to a particular task. Rather than send every page and image directly to a large model, the demo offloads OCR and other document work, then returns a smaller artifact the agent can use.

Makraduli walks through the host, MCP server and GPU worker pools that make the workflow possible. Tools support extraction, summarization, question answering and redaction, while the inference layer handles model loading, batching and different workloads sharing the cluster. He connects those infrastructure choices to embeddings, reranking, task specific LoRAs and the possibility of routing work between models already warm on a GPU. The live exercise starts from an inbox of files and asks the agent to process a document through the configured tools. The final discussion tests the privacy claim: if the agent can access raw files before calling the tool, instructions alone may leave a gap. Questions explore separating file access and processing, running a private cluster and evaluating whether the intended boundary actually holds. The workshop leaves both a working integration and a clear set of constraints to check before using it with sensitive material.

items.title: Parsing the Epstein Files for JMail — Palak Agarwal & Omar Alhait, Reducto
items.description:
Handwritten flight logs and heavily redacted PDFs stand between a pile of documents and a searchable product. Palak Agarwal and Omar Alhait show how Reducto turned the Epstein files into structured data for JMail and its related applications. Agarwal introduces the document processing layer; Alhait walks through the extraction pipeline behind JFlights, showing how a schema turns difficult pages into usable records. The workflow starts with parsing, tests extraction results in Studio, and exposes the configured pipeline through an API call or code snippet. The product demonstration makes the bottleneck visible: reading order, handwriting, layout, and inconsistent documents need to survive extraction before an interface can make them useful.

A live resume example shows how to generate a JSON schema, upload documents, and inspect the resulting fields. The discussion distinguishes a quick schema from one informed by parsed document content, then explores nested fields, citations, figures, and the choice between OCR and PDF metadata. Alhait also describes why drawing a black box over text can leave information exposed, and how the team handled material intended to remain redacted. Questions move from model training and document specific configurations to practical evaluation: inspect a small sample first, then build a representative benchmark before scaling. The recording ends with instructions for an interactive extraction exercise, connecting the JMail case study to participants' own document workflows.

items.title: Building AI Agents with Real-Time Web Data — Yohan Raju, Bright Data
items.description:
A product intelligence agent checks an Amazon listing, searches Reddit for discussion of the same tumbler and turns both sources into a purchase recommendation. Yohan Raju builds that workflow with Bright Data APIs and Gemini, showing why an agent needs fresh, structured evidence rather than relying entirely on information already stored in a model or retrieval system. The demo collects prices, ratings and product details, adds customer sentiment, then asks the model to explain its recommendation. The result is a small example of a wider problem: getting reliable web data into an agent at the moment it needs it.

Before the notebook exercise, Raju walks through the work behind a scraping pipeline: discovering pages, handling changing selectors, managing browser and proxy infrastructure, validating returned fields and delivering clean records downstream. He compares that process with agent driven collection and introduces Bright Data's MCP server as an interface to search, page extraction and browser tools. A side by side Glassdoor example shows the access problem that can interrupt a seemingly simple request. Job data provides another use case, where changes in openings, salaries and locations require continuous updates alongside historical records. The workshop closes with the live notebook results and a discussion of how the same collection and analysis pattern can extend beyond ecommerce.

items.title: RAG Needs a Map: Using GraphRAG to Retrieve Connected Context — Nyah Macklin, Neo4j
items.description:
An agent answering questions about a course needs more than the five chunks closest to a query. It also needs the connections between lessons, concepts, and the sources behind its answer. Nyah Macklin builds that retrieval path with Neo4j, combining vector search with a knowledge graph that people can inspect and query. The workshop starts with the difference between semantic similarity and relationships, then walks through GraphAcademy, an Aura database, and a Python environment. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from course material, embeddings support similarity search, and Cypher exposes the resulting structure. Vectors remain part of the system; the graph adds connected context and a way to answer questions that require traversal or aggregation.

The hands on build moves from a knowledge graph pipeline to an agent in Aura. Macklin creates a vector index, configures a lesson search tool, adds a retrieval query that returns related graph data, and enables natural language questions through text to Cypher. The agent answers a question about temperature using course content and displays its sources. A lesson count prompts a closer check of the underlying database query, showing why visible evidence matters even after the pipeline works. The final code walkthrough covers chunking, entity types, relationship types, and a schema that guides extraction rather than leaving the model to invent the graph's structure.

items.title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
items.description:
Ask a vector store for the PRs you merged last week and it can hand back one that is semantically perfect and three years old. Peter Werry builds context engines at Unblocked, and his thesis is that RAG, meaning similarity search, is only half of retrieval. Engineering context lives in pull requests, review comments, tickets, wikis, and chat, and all of it has structure: authors, dates, states, labels, relationships. Dumping it all in a vector store and reranking fails any question with a temporal or structural half. So the other half is turning natural language into a real database query, where the model does not answer the question, it writes the query. The workshop walks six stacked pull requests that turn a stubbed query playground into a working engine over a GitHub repository.

Four pieces make the query reliable. Schema discovery samples three hundred documents and merges them into one tree, with procedural code rather than a model inferring types and enums. Identity resolution maps Peter to his GitHub login with simple fuzzy matching. Query planning passes the schema, forces a name extraction tool call, and includes the current date. Validation is deny by default: an allow list of operators keeps a function clause from running JavaScript on the server, and hidden metadata fields are wiped and reinjected for tenant isolation. A retry loop feeds validation and execution errors back to the model, which exposes the need for full text search when exact match fails. The same engine then powers a chat agent, and the Q&A covers scaling schemas with summaries, continuous ingestion, why Slack holds the why questions, MCP, and hybrid search.

items.title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
items.description:
Your voice agent's dashboard says it's fast. Your callers say it feels robotic. They're both right.

Jesse Hall, staff developer advocate at LiveKit, explains how to build voice agents that feel human. He shows why leaderboards can't pick your models (scores measure one model, but you ship a pipeline, and errors compound from speech-to-text to the LLM to text-to-speech) and why measured latency isn't what your callers hear. He covers buying time like a person does while tools run, plays a hotel-receptionist demo that handles interruptions and a caller changing his mind, explains LiveKit's audio-based turn detection (4.5% of users cut off vs 9.9% for the best alternative), and lays out the window that matters: a second and a half end to end still works, and around 600 milliseconds starts to feel human. He ends with LiveKit's open-source benchmark you can run against your own agent, a sneak peek of a voice-tuned Gemma model on LiveKit Inference, and a checklist.

In this talk:
• The leaderboard trap, and why pipelines fail differently than models
• Measured vs perceived latency
• Turn detection from audio, and buying time during tool calls
• A latency budget, an open-source benchmark for your agent, and a checklist

items.title: An AI Future Without the Lock-In — Remy Guercio, Tailscale
items.description:
The era of unlimited AI budgets is over, and most teams are locked into whichever tools they picked first.

Remy Guercio, who works on Tailscale's AI gateway Aperture, looks back at a year of AI lock-in and asks how teams get out of it while proving real ROI. He breaks an internal AI deployment into four layers (the models, the data connectors like MCP, CLIs and APIs, the interface, and the sandbox) and argues an AI gateway is what keeps them swappable. He shows how Aperture uses your Tailscale network for identity instead of shared API keys, sets budgets per model (unlimited for cheap models, tight for frontier ones), works as both an LLM and MCP gateway, handles authentication for Cursor, Claude Code and Codex in one place, and keeps logs you can use to diagnose what an agent did.

In this talk:
• Why unlimited AI budgets are ending, and what ROI maxing means
• The four layers of an AI stack and where lock-in hides
• How an AI gateway ties identity, budgets and logs together
• Aperture as both an LLM and MCP gateway

items.title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
items.description:
Most models learn text first and get vision bolted on later. MiniMax M3 learned both from the very first training step.

Olive, who works on reinforcement learning research at MiniMax, goes inside MiniMax M3, an open-weight model with frontier-level coding and agentic ability, a 1 million token context window and native multimodality. She explains MSA, MiniMax's sparse attention design (about 9x faster prefill and 15x faster decoding than full attention): an index branch that picks which blocks matter and a sparse branch that attends only to those, and why existing designs like DeepSeek's DSA didn't fit grouped-query attention or GPU memory access. Then she covers training with text and vision from step zero, why adding vision later gave unstable results, what the attention maps show, and why 3D attention inside the vision transformer improves visual understanding.

In this talk:
• What makes MiniMax M3 different: agentic coding, 1M context, native multimodal
• How MSA sparse attention works, and why DSA didn't fit
• Block-level retrieval and kernels built for real GPUs
• Why training on text and vision from step zero beats adding vision later

items.title: AI Agents Don't Read Your Policy Docs. They Hit Your APIs — Gravitee
items.description:
You can write all the rules you want in a markdown file. Your agent can still call the API.

Sam, CTO at Gravity, skips the slides and runs five live scenarios against a hotel-booking agent to show why governance belongs in the infrastructure, not in the agent's instructions. Running on the Gravity Gateway with a Databricks backend, Sonnet and Groq, he shows the gateway blocking a destructive "delete all bookings" tool call, stopping an attempt to pull every guest's personal data, rate-limiting a buggy agent that fires the same request eight times, serving repeated questions from a semantic cache, and rejecting an oversized prompt before it ever reaches the LLM. He also covers telemetry across your agents, decoupling from any one hyperscaler, trimming bloated MCP tool lists, and shadow AI on employee laptops.

In this talk:
• Why prompts and policy docs can't enforce what agents do
• Blocking destructive tool calls and data exfiltration at the gateway
• Rate limits, semantic caching and token limits that cut cost
• Observability, decoupling from vendors, and trimming MCP tools

items.title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
items.description:
Vector search can't answer "which PRs did I merge last week?" A relational context engine can, and it cuts token burn along the way.

Peter Werry, founding engineer at Unblocked, explains what a context engine is and why coding agents need more than code search: the PRs, Slack threads and incident history that explain why the code is the way it is. He shows Claude sessions with and without that context, including one with about a 50% drop in cost and one that traced a regression to a model switch. Then he builds Unblocked's open-source document query engine step by step: automatic schema discovery, identity resolution across systems, query validation that blocks dangerous operators, retries that feed errors back to the model, and full-text search. He closes with the open-source context engine simulator for testing whether pre-gathered context helps your agents.

In this talk:
• What a context engine is, and how it lowers cost on real agent sessions
• Why vector stores can't answer structural questions about your work
• Turning plain-English questions into safe, validated database queries
• Schema discovery, identity resolution, retries and full-text search

Zero Cold Starts: Serverless AI Agents on Akamai Functions — Thorsten Hans
items.description:
Cold starts, proprietary SDKs and one-region deployments slow AI apps down. WebAssembly at the edge removes all three.

Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate at Akamai, shows how to build and ship MCP servers and AI agents with Spin, the open-source WebAssembly framework, and run them on Akamai Functions, a globally distributed serverless platform with no cold starts. He explains why WebAssembly on the server is fast, portable and sandboxed by default, then live-codes MCP servers with wasmcp: scaffolding tools in TypeScript and Rust, composing them into a full server, testing with MCP Inspector, deploying it worldwide in about 60 seconds with one command, and calling its tools from the Zed editor. He finishes with an agent built on the Vercel AI SDK, backed by a model on a Linode GPU, and explains how memory snapshots keep apps warm.

In this talk:
• Why edge-native beats single-region for AI apps, and how WebAssembly kills cold starts
• What Spin and Akamai Functions are
• Building and composing MCP servers with wasmcp in TypeScript and Rust
• Deploying an MCP server and an AI agent globally with one command

items.title: From Your Laptop to the Pipeline: Scaling Custom Agents with GitHub Copilot
items.description:
Most teams build an agent once, on one laptop, and never share it. Here's how to take it from local to the whole org to the CI pipeline.

Jose Palafox, who has spent six and a half years at GitHub and now works with companies on Copilot adoption, walks through the path from a local custom agent to agents that run unattended in your pipeline. He explains how Copilot works under the hood, the built-in agents in the Copilot CLI, and how to generate and edit a custom agent with the agent builder. Then he shows how to share agents across an organization with a marketplace, run agents across repositories with Orchestrate, and move them into CI with GitHub Agentic Workflows: headless Copilot CLI runs in GitHub Actions, triggered by slash commands in issues, plus a repo with about 200 agents running different parts of the pipeline and agents that investigate their own cost overruns.

In this talk:
• Local vs autonomous agents, and how Copilot works under the hood
• Building custom agents and choosing models for them
• Sharing agents across a company with a marketplace
• Running agents in CI with GitHub Agentic Workflows

items.title: The Lethal Trifecta Is Already on Your Laptops — Michael Patterson, Coder
items.description:
Your coding agent can read private data, take in untrusted content and talk to the internet. That's the lethal trifecta, and it's already running on your developers' laptops.

Michael Patterson, staff solutions engineer at Coder, explains Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally) and why agents like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw running on a laptop hit all three. He covers prompt injection, what blocks big companies from rolling out agents (CISO concerns, shadow AI on personal subscriptions, alert fatigue, skeptical senior engineers), and three architectural guardrails: cloud development environments that isolate the agent, a model proxy that logs traffic and strips sensitive data before it reaches the LLM provider, and an agent firewall that denies commands and domains you didn't allow.

In this talk:
• What the lethal trifecta is, and why laptop agents hit all three parts
• How prompt injection turns trusted sources into attacks
• What security teams worry about when agents roll out at scale
• Three guardrails: cloud dev environments, a model proxy and an agent firewall

items.title: What Most People Get Wrong About Evolution | Akarsh Kumar
items.description:
A lot of people in AI treat evolution as a dumb fallback, basically random search for when you can't take a gradient. Akarsh Kumar thinks that is wrong. Selection hangs on to partial solutions, so mutations only need to be useful about 1% of the time for the search to keep making progress.

Akarsh is a PhD student at MIT working with Phillip Isola, works with Sakana AI, and is first author of the Fractured Entangled Representation paper with Kenneth Stanley, Jeff Clune and Joel Lehman. He tells Tim Scarfe why the path a learner takes may shape the structure of what it learns, and why that is a different way of looking at intelligence from the statistical one.

Most of the conversation is about ASAL, the method he led for searching whole spaces of artificial worlds. Rather than predict what a rule will do, ASAL runs the simulation and asks a foundation model what happened. Mapped across all 262,144 Life-like rules, the most interesting worlds sit on one small island. Along the way: Game of Life, Lenia (with a clip from its creator, Bert Chan), neural cellular automata, Boids, Particle Life and the emergence of persistence.

The last stretch is Core War, a programming game from the 1980s. Asked cold, LLMs write poor Redcode. Used as the mutation step in an evolutionary loop with a verifier, they produced warriors that, between them, beat or tied 96% of 294 human-written ones. Over repeated rounds the warriors trended towards generalists.

---
TIMESTAMPS:
00:00:00 Intro: artificial life, ASAL and Core War in four minutes
00:04:19 Life as it could be, not just as it is
00:05:46 Why the order you learn things in matters
00:08:33 No shortcuts: Wolfram, novelty search and regularisation
00:10:44 Kenneth Stanley: the path matters, not just the destination
00:11:31 Statistical intelligence vs regularity-based intelligence
00:13:49 Artificial chemistry and other possible universes

items.title: From 15% to 90% GPU Utilization: Fix the Data Pipeline, Not the Model
items.description:
Your GPUs might be waiting on your data, not your model. This pipeline went from 15% to 90% GPU utilization.

Tarun Sunkaraneni from Amazon AGI shows that the hardest part of fast multimodal training often isn't the GPU at all, but keeping it fed with data. Training a Qwen3-VL-style model on images stored in S3, the baseline pipeline spent about 85% of its time waiting on data, mostly loading, decoding and resizing images one at a time. He fixes the bottlenecks one by one: concurrency with asyncio and Ray actors, prefetching so data is ready before the trainer asks, and Ray's object store to stop copying big image tensors between processes. Then, at production scale, a new bottleneck appears on a single machine's network card, solved by spreading workers across nodes and using zero-copy reads, which gave another 50% throughput.

In this talk:
• Why multimodal training is often CPU- and IO-bound, not GPU-bound
• Concurrency, prefetching and zero-copy transfer with Ray
• Choosing between asyncio, threads and processes around the GIL
• Why some settings only pay off at scale

items.title: RustConf 2025 Interview: Manish Goregaokar, Rust Devtools
items.description:
At RustConf 2025 in Seattle, the Rust Project Content Team talks with Manish Goregaokar: Clippy co-creator, Servo alum, and around eleven years in the Rust Project, now working on internationalization with ICU4X and interop tooling with Diplomat.

Manish shares how contributing to Servo in 2013-2014, when nightly Rust broke every few weeks, pulled him from working with Rust into working on Rust, and how a silly project full of lints became Clippy. Topics include:

• Clippy's origins and the culture of mentorship inherited from Servo: writing lints as an accessible on-ramp to compiler internals
• How the Rust community changed from one tight-knit group into many overlapping worlds, and why that's healthy
• The surprise of 1.0: the flood of Python and JavaScript developers who were always interested in systems programming once the barrier came down
• An ontology of interop tooling: unidirectional versus bidirectional tools, and why "other languages calling Rust libraries" was the underserved direction
• Diplomat: bridge modules generating a C API, a typed AST, and independently developed backends for C, C++, JavaScript/Wasm, Dart, Kotlin, Java, and Python
• ICU4X: internationalization designed from scratch to be modular, embedded-friendly, and pluggable about data, so your app doesn't mispluralize Polish
• Restraint about writing crates de novo, nerd-sniping yourself, and designs like ZeroVec and Yoke that others had to convince him to build
• jj (Jujutsu): a Rust version control system with changes as first-class concepts distinct from commits
